questions.question: Your Q&A assistant built on qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct knows the formula for the area of a triangle but repeatedly gets multi-step word problems wrong (for example, computing total harvest from a triangular field). Prompt tweaks have not helped. Which approach best addresses the root cause?

options.text: Build a RAG pipeline that retrieves geometry formulas from a math knowledge base
options.explanation: The model already knows the formula; RAG works like an open-book exam and supplies knowledge, but it does not improve logical reasoning, which is what is missing here.

options.text: Increase max_new_tokens so the model has more room to finish its answer
options.explanation: Output length is not the bottleneck; the model fails because it lacks problem-solving ability, not because its answer is cut off.

options.text: Fine-tune the model on expert-written problem-solution examples so it internalizes the reasoning process
options.explanation: Fine-tuning changes the model's parameters so it learns the problem-solving methodology from targeted examples, improving its inherent reasoning ability, which prompts and RAG cannot do.

options.text: Add more few-shot examples to the system prompt until the answers become correct
options.explanation: Prompt engineering only patches around the model; the notebook notes the baseline lacks fundamental problem-solving skills, so prompting alone fails.

questions.takeaway: When the gap is reasoning ability rather than missing knowledge, fine-tuning beats prompt engineering and RAG.

questions.question: A product team wants to fine-tune an LLM for an internal production use case. According to good practice, which checks should be completed before committing to fine-tuning?

options.text: Confirm that the base model has never seen any data similar to the target task during pre-training
options.explanation: This is neither a requirement nor something you can verify; fine-tuning builds on the general knowledge gained in pre-training rather than requiring its absence.

options.text: Confirm that simpler, lower-cost methods such as prompt engineering or a RAG chatbot are not sufficient
options.explanation: Fine-tuning is costly, so cheaper approaches should be evaluated first.

options.text: Confirm that enough high-quality, task-relevant labeled data is available, typically at least 1,000 samples
options.explanation: Below this threshold the model tends to memorize the questions instead of learning the underlying knowledge.

options.text: Confirm that full-parameter fine-tuning is affordable, since PEFT methods cannot reach comparable quality
options.explanation: PEFT methods such as LoRA achieve performance close to full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost, so full fine-tuning affordability is not a prerequisite.

options.text: Confirm that the budget covers the required expertise and infrastructure with acceptable cost-effectiveness
options.explanation: Computational cost and required expertise must align with the project budget.

questions.takeaway: Before fine-tuning: rule out prompt/RAG, secure 1,000+ quality samples, and confirm budget.

questions.question: While training a model f(x) = ax, an engineer computes (y_i - a·x_i)^2 for each sample and then averages these values over all m samples in the training set. What is the averaged quantity called, and why is the difference squared?

options.text: The cost function; squaring prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling out and amplifies larger errors
options.explanation: The cost function measures overall performance across all training samples (here the mean squared error), and squaring avoids cancellation while amplifying errors.

options.text: The loss function; squaring makes the value easier to compute on a GPU
options.explanation: The per-sample error is the loss function; the average over all samples is the cost function, and squaring is not about GPU convenience.

options.text: The gradient; squaring gives the direction of steepest ascent
options.explanation: The gradient is the slope used to choose the update direction, not the averaged squared error.

options.text: The learning rate; squaring keeps the step size positive
options.explanation: The learning rate is a coefficient that scales the step size; it is not computed from prediction errors.

questions.takeaway: Loss measures error on one sample; cost averages it over the training set, and training means minimizing it.

sources.heading: 2.1.2 loss function & Cost function - quantifying model performance

questions.question: During gradient descent on a high-dimensional loss surface, in which direction should the parameters be adjusted at each step to approach the minimum fastest?

options.text: In the direction of the gradient, because it points to the steepest change
options.explanation: The gradient points toward the steepest ascent, so moving along it increases the loss.

options.text: In a randomly chosen direction, refined with a fixed step size
options.explanation: Randomness is only used for the starting point; fixed step sizes can cause oscillation around the minimum.

options.text: Along whichever single parameter axis has the largest value
options.explanation: The update considers the partial derivatives for all parameters together, not just one axis chosen by value.

options.text: Opposite to the gradient, which is the direction of steepest descent
options.explanation: The gradient points to the steepest ascent, so its opposite is the steepest descent and leads to the lowest point fastest.

questions.takeaway: Gradient descent steps against the gradient, scaled by the learning rate.

questions.question: Which statements about the learning rate in LLM fine-tuning are accurate?

options.text: A larger learning rate is always preferable because it reaches the minimum in fewer steps
options.explanation: An excessively high learning rate can overshoot the optimum and never converge, and can destroy what the pretrained model learned.

options.text: It is a coefficient multiplied by the slope to regulate the size of each parameter update
options.explanation: The learning rate scales the slope to control step size, preventing oscillation on steep loss curves.

options.text: Once training starts, the learning rate must remain constant to guarantee convergence
options.explanation: Dynamic adjustment is common in practice; ms-swift even applies learning rate decay automatically to improve convergence stability.

options.text: For LoRA fine-tuning of large models, it is typically in the range of 1e-5 to 5e-4
options.explanation: This range is much smaller than training from scratch because only small adjustments to the pretrained model are needed.

questions.takeaway: Pick a small learning rate for fine-tuning: too high diverges, too low wastes compute.

questions.question: You start a LoRA fine-tuning run with learning_rate=0.1, lora_rank=4, and num_train_epochs=1 on 100 samples. Both training loss and validation loss rise during training. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase num_train_epochs so the model has more time to converge
options.explanation: Rising training loss means the model is not learning at all; more epochs would just prolong a failed setup.

options.text: Significantly reduce the learning rate, for example to 0.00005
options.explanation: Training loss rising indicates training failure, almost always from a learning rate that is too high; a much smaller step lets the loss decrease smoothly.

options.text: Increase lora_rank so the model has more learning capacity
options.explanation: Rank controls capacity, but the parameters are oscillating due to oversized steps, which rank does not fix.

options.text: Add more training data, because rising validation loss indicates overfitting
options.explanation: Overfitting shows training loss falling while validation loss rises; here training loss also rises, which signals training failure.

questions.takeaway: Training loss that rises or stays flat signals a failed setup, most often a learning rate that is too high.

questions.question: After a fine-tuning run finishes, both training loss and validation loss are still steadily decreasing at the final step. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: The model is underfitting and should be allowed to train longer, for example by increasing the number of epochs
options.explanation: Both losses still dropping means the model is improving but has not yet fully captured the patterns; continuing training is the fix.

options.text: The model is overfitting and the number of epochs should be reduced
options.explanation: Overfitting is indicated by validation loss rising while training loss falls, not by both decreasing.

options.text: Training has failed, and the learning rate should be lowered
options.explanation: Training failure shows training loss unchanged or rising; here it is decreasing as expected.

options.text: Training has succeeded, and the last checkpoint is optimal
options.explanation: Since validation loss is still improving, the model has not yet reached its best performance.

questions.takeaway: Both losses falling at the end of training means underfitting: train longer.

questions.question: In a fine-tuning run on 100 samples for 50 epochs, training loss keeps dropping while validation loss starts rising partway through. The model answers training questions verbatim but fails on rephrased ones. Which actions help address this?

options.text: Increase num_train_epochs so the model can move past the memorization phase
options.explanation: More epochs deepen memorization; the validation loss would continue to rise.

options.text: Reduce num_train_epochs
options.explanation: Fewer epochs give the model less opportunity to memorize the training data.

options.text: Greatly increase lora_rank while keeping the same 100 samples
options.explanation: A high rank with little data makes memorization even more likely, worsening overfitting.

options.text: Increase the amount and diversity of training data, for example to 1,000+ samples
options.explanation: More varied data makes rote memorization insufficient, forcing the model to learn the underlying knowledge.

options.text: Use early stopping by monitoring eval loss and halting when it starts rising
options.explanation: Early stopping stops training at the overfitting turning point instead of using a fixed epoch count.

questions.takeaway: Fix overfitting with fewer epochs, more diverse data, or early stopping, not more capacity.

questions.question: A LoRA fine-tuning job crashes with a CUDA out-of-memory error at batch_size=16. You want the gradient stability of a batch of 16 while staying within memory limits. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: batch_size=1 with no other changes
options.explanation: Batch size 1 produces a very noisy loss curve because gradients estimated from a single sample are highly random.

options.text: batch_size=16 with max_length doubled
options.explanation: A longer max_length makes each sample consume more memory, worsening OOM.

options.text: batch_size=4 with lora_rank increased to 64
options.explanation: A higher rank adds parameters and memory use, and does not provide the effect of a larger batch.

options.text: batch_size=4 with gradient_accumulation_steps=4
options.explanation: Gradient accumulation gives the effective behavior of batch_size=16 while using only the memory footprint of batch_size=4.

questions.takeaway: Gradient accumulation trades extra steps for large-batch stability without the memory cost.

questions.question: An architect is comparing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods. Which statements are accurate?

options.text: PEFT methods update all model weights but at reduced precision to save memory
options.explanation: PEFT updates only a small subset of parameters and keeps most original weights frozen.

options.text: LoRA requires modifying the internal architecture of the model and therefore always slows down inference
options.explanation: LoRA does not depend on the internal architecture, and its matrices can be merged so inference efficiency is unaffected.

options.text: Adapter Tuning inserts small trainable modules into the model and adds extra computation during inference
options.explanation: Adapters require structural changes and introduce inference overhead due to the extra layers.

options.text: Prompt Tuning learns soft prompt embeddings while the original model parameters remain frozen
options.explanation: Only the learnable input vectors are updated; the model architecture is not modified.

options.text: The Freeze method updates only a small portion of parameters, such as the final layers, and may underperform on tasks very different from pre-training
options.explanation: Freeze is highly parameter-efficient but has limited adaptability for complex or divergent tasks.

questions.takeaway: PEFT methods freeze most weights; they differ in where the trainable parameters live and their inference cost.

questions.question: Your training samples vary widely in length, and GPU memory is tight. How should max_length be chosen?

options.text: Set it to the length of the longest sample so no sample is ever truncated
options.explanation: Covering extreme outliers makes every sample consume more memory and risks OOM errors.

options.text: Set it as low as possible to maximize batch_size, since truncation does not affect quality
options.explanation: Truncation makes the model learn from incomplete information, which hurts quality.

options.text: Check the length distribution and set it to cover the vast majority (95%+) of samples
options.explanation: This balances quality and memory; any memory freed can then be traded for a larger batch_size.

options.text: Leave it unset, because max_length only affects inference, not training memory
options.explanation: max_length caps each training sample's length and directly affects memory consumption during training.

questions.takeaway: Size max_length from the data's length distribution (~95% coverage) and trade it off against batch_size.

questions.question: You plan a 50-epoch fine-tuning run with ms-swift. What is the main benefit of choosing an appropriate eval_steps value?

options.text: It increases the learning rate automatically whenever validation loss plateaus
options.explanation: eval_steps controls evaluation frequency; it does not modify the learning rate.

options.text: It lets you detect the overfitting turning point early, and ms-swift keeps the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss as best_model_checkpoint
options.explanation: Periodic evaluation reveals when eval loss starts rising, and the framework saves a checkpoint at each evaluation and marks the best one.

options.text: Evaluating at every single step is recommended because it has no impact on training speed
options.explanation: Evaluating too frequently noticeably slows training; a guideline is every 5–10% of total steps.

options.text: It determines how many samples are used per gradient update
options.explanation: That is batch_size; eval_steps is the number of training steps between validation evaluations.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate every 5–10% of training steps so overfitting is caught and the best checkpoint is preserved.

questions.question: A model has a hidden dimension d = 1536. For a single d × d weight matrix, how many trainable parameters does LoRA with rank r = 8 introduce, compared with full-parameter fine-tuning of that matrix?

options.explanation: 12,288 counts only one of the two LoRA matrices (1536 × 8); LoRA trains both A and B.
This reverses the two figures; full fine-tuning trains all 1536 × 1536 parameters.

options.text: 24,576 versus 2,359,296, a saving of about 98.96%
options.explanation: LoRA trains A (1536 × 8) plus B (8 × 1536) = 24,576 parameters versus 1536 × 1536 = 2,359,296 for the full matrix.
This would correspond to rank 64 for both matrices, not rank 8.

questions.takeaway: LoRA trainable parameters per matrix = 2 × d × r, a tiny fraction of d².

questions.question: Which statements correctly describe how LoRA works?

options.text: It directly overwrites the original weight matrix, so the base model cannot be recovered after training
options.explanation: LoRA does not modify the original weights; rollback only requires removing the added low-rank matrices.

options.text: The pre-trained weights stay frozen while two small trainable matrices A (d × r) and B (r × d) model the weight update
options.explanation: LoRA approximates the update as a low-rank product A·B added to the frozen pre-trained weights.

options.text: It requires inserting new adapter layers between transformer blocks
options.explanation: That describes Adapter Tuning; LoRA does not depend on the internal architecture.

options.text: At inference, A, B and the pre-trained weights can be merged statically or dynamically without affecting inference efficiency
options.explanation: Merging produces a single fine-tuned weight matrix, so no extra inference cost is incurred.

options.text: It relies on the assumption that adapting to a downstream task requires only a low-rank weight change
options.explanation: Pre-training captures high-rank general knowledge, while fine-tuning updates are assumed to be low-rank.

questions.takeaway: LoRA adds a mergeable low-rank update to frozen weights, so it is cheap to train and easy to revert.

questions.question: You are choosing the LoRA rank r for several projects. Which guidelines are consistent with best practice?

options.text: Choose r proportional to model size, so a 175B model needs a far larger rank than a 1.5B model
options.explanation: The LoRA paper found r = 1 or 2 sufficient for GPT-3 175B; optimal r does not scale proportionally with model size.

options.text: For a small dataset (about 1k–10k samples), keep r at or below 16 to reduce the risk of overfitting
options.explanation: A high rank with limited data encourages memorization rather than generalization.

options.text: For simple tasks such as format conversion or style transfer, r of 4–8 is usually sufficient
options.explanation: Simple tasks need little extra capacity, so a small rank works.

options.text: When the dataset grows substantially, a somewhat larger r can help the model absorb the additional knowledge
options.explanation: Rank should match data volume; in the experiments, rank rose from 4 to 8 when data grew from 100 to 1,000 samples.

options.text: For complex tasks such as cross-lingual transfer or domain-specific reasoning, a larger r such as 16–64 may be needed
options.explanation: Complex tasks have richer features to capture, which benefits from more LoRA capacity.

questions.takeaway: Match LoRA rank to data volume, task complexity, and memory, not to raw model size.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts pre-training and fine-tuning?

options.text: Pre-training uses small labeled datasets, while fine-tuning uses massive unlabeled web text
options.explanation: This reverses the data: pre-training uses large-scale general data, fine-tuning uses small task-specific data.

options.text: Both pre-training and fine-tuning always update all model parameters
options.explanation: Fine-tuning can update only part of the parameters, as in PEFT methods.

options.text: Fine-tuning learns general features, while pre-training adapts the model to a specific task
options.explanation: The objectives are reversed: pre-training learns general features, fine-tuning adapts to specific tasks.

options.text: Pre-training is generally self-supervised on large general data, while fine-tuning is supervised on smaller task-specific annotated data
options.explanation: Pre-training needs no manual annotation, whereas fine-tuning uses labeled task data, typically a few thousand to tens of thousands of samples.

questions.takeaway: Pre-train self-supervised on broad data; fine-tune supervised on a small labeled task set.

questions.question: In a fine-tuning workflow, which statements correctly describe the roles of the data splits?

options.text: The training set is used to compute training loss, which drives parameter updates via gradient descent
options.explanation: Like a practice workbook, the model learns from it and updates parameters based on its loss.

options.text: The test set should be merged into the training set to maximize the data available for learning
options.explanation: The test set represents the real exam and must stay separate to measure final performance fairly.

options.text: The validation set is used periodically during training to compute validation loss and judge how training is progressing
options.explanation: Like a mock exam, validation loss shows performance on unseen but similar data.

options.text: The validation loss is what the optimizer minimizes directly when updating weights
options.explanation: Parameters are updated from the training loss; validation loss is only monitored.

options.text: Accuracy on the test set is used to evaluate the model's final overall performance
options.explanation: The test set is used for the final evaluation, as in the post-fine-tuning exam.

questions.takeaway: Train on the training set, monitor with the validation set, and judge final quality on a held-out test set.

questions.question: After fine-tuning with ms-swift, you want to ship a standalone model that can be served without PEFT libraries. What should you do?

options.text: Run swift export with --merge_lora true on the best_model_checkpoint to merge the LoRA weights into the base model
options.explanation: Merging produces a complete model with updated parameters that can be deployed independently.

options.text: Deploy the last_model_checkpoint adapter alone, since LoRA weights contain the full model
options.explanation: The roughly 20 MB adapter holds only low-rank matrices and must be loaded with the base model.

options.text: Load the adapter dynamically onto any available base model, since LoRA weights are model-agnostic
options.explanation: With dynamic loading you must specify the same base model that was used for fine-tuning.

options.text: Retrain the model with full-parameter fine-tuning, because LoRA results cannot be merged
options.explanation: LoRA matrices can be merged with the base weights statically, so retraining is unnecessary.

questions.takeaway: Ship a merged model via swift export --merge_lora, or load the small adapter onto its exact base model.

questions.question: Your team is building a fine-tuning dataset for a complex domain task. Which practices are recommended?

options.text: Duplicate the existing 300 samples several times to exceed the 1,000-sample threshold
options.explanation: Duplication adds no new information and encourages memorization; the threshold refers to high-quality, diverse samples.

options.text: Remove noisy, ambiguous, or incorrect entries that could mislead training
options.explanation: Data quality requires accurate, relevant, error-free samples.

options.text: Cover a wide range of scenarios, contexts, and domain terminology
options.explanation: Diversity prevents overfitting to a narrow data distribution.

options.text: Restrict the data to a single representative scenario so the model learns it deeply
options.explanation: A narrow distribution invites overfitting and poor generalization.

options.text: Expand the data with expert annotation, LLM-generated synthetic data, or external sources, and iterate based on validation performance
options.explanation: These are recommended expansion strategies, and continuous iteration on the dataset is part of the process.

questions.takeaway: Fine-tuning data should be accurate, diverse, balanced, and iteratively improved, typically 1,000+ samples.

questions.question: You fine-tuned a model for document summarization and want an automatic metric that compares generated summaries with reference summaries. Which metric is most appropriate?

options.text: Intersection over Union (IoU)
options.explanation: IoU measures bounding-box overlap in object detection, not text quality.

options.text: ROUGE
options.explanation: ROUGE is commonly used for summarization and measures n-gram recall, precision, and F-measure against references.

options.text: mAP (mean average precision)
options.explanation: mAP is a standard object detection metric across classes and confidence thresholds.

options.text: Perplexity, where a higher value indicates better summaries
options.explanation: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts a sample, and lower perplexity is better, not higher.

questions.takeaway: Choose evaluation metrics by task type: ROUGE for summarization, BLEU for translation, accuracy/F1 for classification.
